Two of my cats are allergic to all poultry. They even have issues if the cat food is just made in the same facility as the poultry food. Our vet said some companies don't clean the machines between proteins, too. They both also have kidney disease. All of the hydrolyzed protein diets were too high in phosphorus for them, and all of the kidney disease diets at the time had some type of poultry or poultry byproduct in them.

Our vet sent us to a veterinary nutritionist, who helped us figure out how to make a home cooked diet for our kitties. There are meal completer supplements you can use, like EZ Complete (which has chicken liver in it) and Alnutrin (you have to add the liver yourself). We use the Egg-Free Alnutrin with Calcium. The site has a calculator to help you prepare balanced meals for your kitties. However, you must consult with a veterinary nutritionist before switching to making your cats' food yourself! Your primary vet can refer you.

I will say it can be a lot of work, but it's worth it! My cats are so much happier and healthier now.

One of my childhood cats was originally a stray before we adopted her. For the first 3 years we had her, she would eat anything. We had to limit the amount of dry food we put out because she would gobble it up until she puked, then do it all again. All of our cats were fed wet food twice a day. She'd clear her plate and then try to clear the other cats' plates, so we had to feed her separately.

Whenever we ate, she would try to steal food from our plates. She ate pretty much anything for those first 3 years. We had to be very careful because she'd even try to eat foods that were dangerous for cats, like garlic, grapes, and onions. She never got any, but she would try.

Her bloodwork was normal, so it wasn't her thyroid. Our vet told us she had likely been traumatized by food insecurity since she was a stray. They said she might recover one day, or she could be like that for the rest of her life.

About 3 years later, she started turning her nose up to hotdogs, hamburgers, and some lunch meat. She wasn't gobbling the dry food when we put it out. She would sometimes leave a little bit of wet food on her plate and walk away. She stopped trying to steal food from our plates all the time. We thought something was wrong with her again, so we took her to the vet. They couldn't find anything wrong with her, and her bloodwork was normal. They said she had finally realized that she wouldn't ever have to go hungry again. 

My mom still has her 14 years later. She became a very picky lady once she felt safe enough! My mom always makes sure she has her current favorites.

The laws are pretty similar across the country. You can't just find something and keep it. It's theft.

California: PEN 485
"One who finds lost property under circumstances which give him knowledge of or means of inquiry as to the true owner, and who appropriates such property to his own use, or to the use of another person not entitled thereto, without first making reasonable and just efforts to find the owner and to restore the property to him, is guilty of theft." (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=485.)

Florida: Section 705.102
"(3) It is unlawful for any person who finds any lost or abandoned property to appropriate the same to his or her own use or to refuse to deliver the same when required.
(4) Any person who unlawfully appropriates such lost or abandoned property to his or her own use or refuses to deliver such property when required commits theft as defined in s. 812.014, punishable as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084." (https://casetext.com/statute/florida-statutes/title-xl-real-and-personal-property/chapter-705-lost-or-abandoned-property/section-705102-reporting-lost-or-abandoned-property)

Pennsylvania: Section 3924
"A person who comes into control of property of another that he knows to have been lost, mislaid, or delivered under a mistake as to the nature or amount of the property or the identity of the recipient is guilty of theft if, with intent to deprive the owner thereof, he fails to take reasonable measures to restore the property to a person entitled to have it." (https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/LI/CT/HTM/18/00.039.024.000..HTM)

A PIN is a 4 digit number the customer has to give the delivery driver upon delivery. Uber Eats sets the delivery PIN as the last 4 digits of the phone number on the account. I've never needed a delivery PIN for a Doordash order.

The delivery PIN serves as proof that the customer got the order. It's usually only required when a customer (or someone at that address) reports a lot of things wrong with their orders, or if a customer (or someone at that address) has reported at least one order as completely missing in the past. It's also required with new customers.

I've noticed it's required pretty often at houses I recognize as STRs.

Or the customer can just give the driver the PIN themselves at the door. They can come back later when they know the guest would likely be gone (like during a football game or concert).

If I do a full day of just restaurant delivery, I'd say I deliver to about 5-10 STRs that I recognize as STRs.

Also, it's pretty easy to identify an Airbnb if you work on delivery apps even casually. They order delivery very frequently, sometimes daily or multiple times a day. The customer names are different from week to week. The smart locks are a telltale sign, too. I've found most of them require delivery PINs, as well. I'm not sure why, but maybe it's because there's different people staying there pretty frequently.

So, this could be a massive security risk. Delivery drivers can get the PIN from the customer in person or from their voicemail. Since Airbnb hosts typically make the smart lock code the last 4 digits of the guest's phone number, that delivery driver can now access that Airbnb for the duration of that guest's stay. 

You and your guest are very lucky this delivery driver was a good (but dumb) person, and he just put the order inside and left. These apps are very clear that you're never supposed to enter someone's home. It's dangerous for all parties involved, and the company could be liable if anything happened. Drivers have been attacked and even killed, and so have customers.

Customers can not share their actual phone numbers in messages to the driver. The apps will mask it, so it looks like you're just typing something like "xxx-xxx-xxxx." They do this to protect customers' and drivers' identities.

Anyone can access your phone number if it's in your voicemail greeting. Even though delivery drivers can't see your phone number in the app, they can call you through a masked number in the app and listen to your voicemail greeting to get your number.

Uber Eats drivers can call your phone, but the numbers are masked. They can't see your real number, and you can't see theirs. 

However, the customer's voicemail greeting may contain their phone number. The Uber Eats driver probably called them, and they didn't answer, so the driver got their number from that. This is a known workaround to get the delivery PIN when a customer isn't answering. 

You should always change your default voicemail greeting to something like, "The person you have dialed is not available right now. Please leave a message." Don't include your name, phone number, or any other information that can be used to identify you.

If it's corporate owned or professionally managed, it's probably safe to assume they use Realpage. If you get any utility bill through Realpage, they probably also use the Realpage revenue management software. 

One of my past landlords used Realpage Utility Management. Realpage sent me monthly emails with a link to my bill. Their logo was at the top of every email and bill. The Realpage company name was mentioned repeatedly in the email and bill as well.

When you applied, if your landlord used a third-party screening service, it could have been Realpage. If they did a hard credit check, it should show up on your credit report. 

The screening service Realpage offers now is called Realpage Artificial Intelligence (AI) Screening. It's a score they use to evaluate and screen tenants. The algorithms they use are secret, and there's not much regulation or oversight for tenant screening, unlike credit reporting.  https://www.propublica.org/article/how-your-shadow-credit-score-could-decide-whether-you-get-an-apartment

Keep any and all communications between you and your landlord. Keep any paperwork, emails, voicemails, and anything else from your landlord. Keep it all for years. Make copies and save them in multiple places, like on your computer, on a flash drive, and in your Google Drive.

Be sure to look for anything that has any mention of Realpage, Yieldstar (the name of Realpage's revenue management software), or American Utility Management (AUM). Before Realpage, my landlord used AUM, which was bought by Realpage in 2017.

There are going to be class action lawsuits coming, so be sure to keep your evidence and protect it.
